source.title: Finding Memo: Extractive Memorization in Constrained Sequence Generation Tasks

record.tranche_reason: The study measures extractive memorization and its effects in neural machine translation. It does not test any listed claim version about random-label fitting, generalization gaps, architecture or optimizer conditions, sharpness measures, or removal of influential examples.
record.gate_note: The study's results concern a different operational definition of memorization in translation. Its generalization statements in the introduction cite prior work; they are not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures extractive memorization in translation, defined by reproducing a training reference from a shortened source prefix. It does not test random-label fitting (V1), removal of counterfactually memorized examples (V8), or any architecture, width, optimizer, batch, dropout, or sharpness comparison in V2–V7. Its discussion of generalization and counterfactual memorization cites prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that prefix-based extraction identifies memorization threatening NMT reliability, that a symbol-prefix procedure can recover alternative translations, and that finetuning on recovered outputs can impart corrective behavior while preserving general quality. These are claims about extractive memorization and its mitigation, not tests of V1–V8.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates extractive memorization in NMT using prefix-based extraction and perturbation methods; it does not use the original methods in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The neighborhood effect varies by perturbation position; prefix and suffix perturbations differ, and perturbing the first token often changes the output. Recovery results vary with the chosen symbol. The prefix-ratio threshold changes the quantity and quality of extracted samples.

fits_no_version.finding: The En-De model reproduced references from shortened prefixes for 520/208,242 examined training samples. The authors report repetition-associated extraction rates and lower aggregate COMET-QE for extracted samples. Their lexical-diversity interpretation requires caution because TTR differs across unequal-sized sets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prefix-based extractive memorization occurs in this translation system and is associated with training repetition and lower estimated translation quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Memorized translations persisted under 16.65% of prefix, 51.65% of suffix, and 8.00% of first-token perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Translation invariance around extractively memorized inputs depends on perturbation position.

fits_no_version.finding: The best of five recovery symbols elicited alternative translations for 339/520 samples. Subsequent finetuning increased reported test BLEU from 32.9 to 33.5 and COMET-QE on F from 54.57 to 68.94.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prefix-symbol recovery and finetuning can improve reported translation metrics for this system.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study uses one primary En-De Transformer-Big system for its main experiments. The authors say the prefix-ratio threshold was selected based on initial En-De experiments and should ideally depend on language-pair length ratios; higher thresholds increase quantity and quality but can introduce false positives. They state that they did not compare data-filtering algorithms and that their mitigation approach may not be optimal.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were extracted for the additional language-pair tables, detailed repetition-bucket quality scores, individual perturbation buckets, or example-based transferable attacks. The main results above capture the reported aggregate findings relevant to the study's distinct extractive-memorization construct; none test the listed versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy under matched architectures and training recipes.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification, including local connectivity and initialization effects.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under different tuning and regularization conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout effects on held-out error across training-set sizes and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps against alternative measures.
Removing examples selected by counterfactual label memorization and comparing retrained test accuracy with matched random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; this does not negate the reported extractive-memorization findings. No version-relevant omitted results were found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Large-batch versus small-batch training and recipe changes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps.
Removing influential memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.
